# ECON 0100 | Demo C | Solutions

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

## Flummoxed by the Floo Powder Fiasco

Floo Powder is a magical commodity used by witches and wizards to transport themselves through fireplaces to different locations. While it's often convenient, its use is associated with negative environmental effects, including air pollution and the depletion of magical resources used to produce the powder. The Ministry's Bureau of Economic Analysis has estimated the externality to be ~~10 galleons~~ {++15 coins per tin++} with the following supply and demand equations:

$$
P_b = 120 - 2 Q_d \qquad\textit{and}\qquad P_s = Q_s
$$

## Q1 | The Fiasco (C1.1)

Start by using a graph to describe the market failure. Be sure to graph but don't calculate DWL. No need to discuss other welfare measures. {++Use a graph and algebra to describe the market failure.++}

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=66.667%}

{++a\) Marginal social cost: MSC = **15 + Q** (C1.1)++}

{++b\) Market quantity: **40** c\) Socially efficient quantity: **35** (C1.1)++}

{++d\) On the axes, draw demand, supply, and MSC, and shade the deadweight loss. (C1.1)++}

{++e\) For the last tin traded, MSC = **55** and MB = **40**, so the market trades: **too much**, too little (C1.1)++}

:::

::: {.column width=33.333%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

a\) The sellers' marginal cost is the supply curve, Q. Each tin also costs everyone else 15, so MSC = **15 + Q**: supply shifted up by 15.

b\) The market ignores the external cost and trades where demand meets supply: 120 − 2Q = Q gives Q = **40** at a price of 40.

c\) Efficiency needs MB = MSC: 120 − 2Q = 15 + Q gives 3Q = 105, so Q = **35**, where MB = MSC = 50.

d\) The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and demand over the tins from 35 to 40, with corners (35, 50), (40, 55) and (40, 40). Its area, ½ · 15 · 5 = 37.5, is not required.

e\) At Q = 40, MSC = 15 + 40 = **55** and MB = 120 − 80 = **40**. The last tin costs society 15 more than it is worth to its buyer, and the same is true of every tin from 35 to 40, so the market trades **too much**.

:::

# ECON 0100 | Demo C | Solutions

## Q2 | A Tax for Revenue (C2.1)

{++Needing revenue, and not yet knowing the size of the externality, the Ministry imposes a tax of 6 coins per tin on Floo Powder.++}

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=66.667%}

{++a\) Quantity traded: **38** b\) Price buyers pay: **44** c\) Price sellers receive: **38** (C2.1)++}

{++d\) Compared with the untaxed price, buyers pay **4** more per tin and sellers receive **2** less (C2.1)++}

{++e\) The side that bears more of the tax: **buyers**, sellers (C2.1)++}

:::

::: {.column width=33.333%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

a\) The tax opens a wedge of 6 between the two prices: Pb − Ps = 6. Substituting the curves, (120 − 2Q) − Q = 6, so 3Q = 114 and Q = **38**.

b\) Buyers pay Pb = 120 − 2 · 38 = **44**.

c\) Sellers receive Ps = **38**. Check: 44 − 38 = 6.

d\) Without the tax the price is 40. Buyers pay 44 − 40 = **4** more, and sellers receive 40 − 38 = **2** less. The two burdens add to the tax.

e\) **Buyers** bear more, 4 of the 6 coins. Demand is steeper than supply (slope 2 against 1), so buyers are the side less able to move away from the tax.

:::

\newpage

# ECON 0100 | Demo C | Solutions

## Q3 | Designing the Policy (C3.1)

The Ministry of Magic has hired you to design a policy that corrects the market failure caused by the negative externality of Floo Powder use. Discuss the policy intervention you would recommend, how it would impact the market for Floo Powder and its users, and the government's welfare associated with the policy.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=66.667%}

{++a\) Policy type: **tax**, subsidy Policy size: **15** per tin (C3.1)++}

{++b\) Quantity traded with your policy: **35** (C3.1)++}

{++c\) The 6-coin tax in Q2 left the quantity at **38**, which is: **above**, at, below the socially efficient quantity (C3.1)++}

:::

::: {.column width=33.333%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

a\) The externality is a cost, so the policy is a **tax**, and its size is the external cost per tin, **15**. Sellers then pay the full social cost: supply plus the tax is 15 + Q, which is exactly MSC.

b\) With the wedge Pb − Ps = 15: (120 − 2Q) − Q = 15 gives Q = **35**, the efficient quantity. Buyers pay 50 and sellers receive 35 (not required).

c\) The 6-coin tax moved quantity from 40 to **38**, the right direction but not far enough: 38 is still **above** the efficient 35, because the tax is smaller than the external cost. The tins from 35 to 38 still cost society more than they are worth.

:::

# ECON 0100 | Demo C | Solutions

## Patronus Lessons

{++Every winter, dementors drift through Hogsmeade, and the surest defense against them is the Patronus Charm. Private tutors sell lessons in the charm. Each witch or wizard who learns it also protects their neighbors from dementors, an external benefit of 6 coins per lesson. Prices are in coins and quantity is in lessons. The demand (marginal private benefit) and supply (marginal cost) equations for lessons are the following:++}

$$
P_b = 40 - \frac{1}{2} Q_d \qquad\textit{and}\qquad P_s = 10 + \frac{1}{4} Q_s
$$

## Q4 | Patronus Lessons (C1.2)

{++The graph shows the market for lessons: marginal private benefit (MPB), marginal social benefit (MSB), and supply (S). The lettered regions are for the questions.++}

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=55%}

{++a\) MSB lies **6** coins above MPB at every quantity (C1.2)++}

{++b\) Market quantity: **40** (C1.2)++}

{++c\) Socially efficient quantity: **48** (C1.2)++}

{++d\) Deadweight-loss region (letter): **B** (C1.2)++}

{++e\) The market trades: too many, **too few** lessons (C1.2)++}

:::

::: {.column width=45%}

![Market for Patronus lessons with MPB, MSB and S; region B, the deadweight loss, is shaded red](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

a\) Each lesson is worth its buyer MPB and is worth another **6** to the neighbors it protects, so MSB = MPB + 6 = 46 − Q/2, a parallel line **6** above MPB.

b\) Buyers count only their own benefit, so the market trades where MPB meets supply: 40 − Q/2 = 10 + Q/4 gives Q = **40** at a price of 20. On the graph, the left tick.

c\) Efficiency needs MSB = MC: 46 − Q/2 = 10 + Q/4 gives Q = **48**, where MSB = MC = 22. The right tick.

d\) **B**: the triangle between MSB and supply over the lessons from 40 to 48. Each of those lessons is worth more to society than it costs, yet none is traded. A is the external benefit the 40 traded lessons already deliver. C, between supply and MPB, is how far each of lessons 41 to 48 costs more than its buyer alone would pay, the reason the market skips them; it is not a loss to society.

e\) **Too few**: at 40, the last lesson has MSB = 26 and MC = 20, so one more lesson would add 6 more in benefit than it costs.

:::

\newpage

# ECON 0100 | Demo C | Solutions

## Q5 | A Subsidy for Lessons (C2.2)

{++To encourage lessons, the Ministry pays tutors a subsidy of 9 coins per lesson.++}

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=66.667%}

{++a\) Quantity traded: **52** (C2.2)++}

{++b\) Price buyers pay: **14** c\) Price sellers receive: **23** (C2.2)++}

{++d\) For the last lesson traded, MC = **23** and MSB = **20**, so MC is: **above**, below MSB (C2.2)++}

:::

::: {.column width=33.333%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

a\) The subsidy reverses the wedge: sellers receive 9 more than buyers pay, Ps − Pb = 9. Substituting, (10 + Q/4) − (40 − Q/2) = 9, so 3Q/4 = 39 and Q = **52**.

b\) Buyers pay Pb = 40 − 52/2 = **14**.

c\) Sellers receive Ps = 10 + 52/4 = **23**. Check: 23 − 14 = 9.

d\) At Q = 52, MC = **23** and MSB = 46 − 26 = **20**, so MC is **above** MSB. The subsidy of 9 is larger than the external benefit of 6, so it pushes past the efficient 48: lessons 49 to 52 cost more than they are worth to society, the small red triangle. A subsidy of exactly 6 would stop at 48.

:::
